Resident count alone cannot establish daily demand or peak capacity. Obtain available fuels, energy tariffs and budget before comparing operating costs or estimating savings.

2. **Survey the site and develop the system layout.**  
   Establish usable, unshaded roof area, orientation, slope, structural capacity, pipe routes and plant-room space. Obtain local solar-resource and weather data. These determine feasible collector area, collector type, storage volume and achievable solar contribution; finalize none without assessment. A candidate arrangement is: **cold supply → solar preheat storage → backup heater → thermostatic mixing valve → taps**. Collectors transfer heat to storage, potentially through a separate fluid loop and heat exchanger. Include appropriate pumps, differential-temperature controls, insulation, isolation valves, expansion vessels, backflow protection and safely discharged pressure/temperature relief devices.

3. **Define seasonal operation and backup provision.**  
   Model monthly performance against measured demand rather than assuming year-round solar coverage. Controls should circulate heat only when collectors can usefully warm storage. Backup heating must meet the required service level during prolonged cloud, winter conditions or solar-system downtime; its capacity depends on peak demand and available storage. Minimum temperatures and water quality govern whether direct circulation, an indirect antifreeze loop or properly designed drainback is suitable. Address summer overheating, stagnation and low-occupancy periods with compatible equipment and engineered protection—not routine hot-water dumping.

4. **Resolve installation and maintenance risks before procurement.**  
   Obtain structural approval and applicable plumbing, electrical and building permissions. Qualified installers should address roof waterproofing, wind/snow loads, safe roof access, hot pipework, leaks and electrical protection. Check water hardness and chemistry for scaling, corrosion and heat-exchanger compatibility. Prevent contamination between heat-transfer fluid and potable water. Provide scald protection and code-compliant Legionella controls for both preheat and final storage. Plan accessible servicing of collectors, pumps, valves, sensors, anodes and heat-transfer fluid, with inspection intervals based on manufacturer guidance and local conditions.

5. **Commission, monitor and verify performance.**  
   Pressure-test circuits; verify relief devices, mixing temperatures, controls, freeze/overheat protection and backup operation. Confirm adequate hot water during peak demand and check insulation and recirculation losses. Meter useful solar heat, auxiliary energy, water flow and relevant temperatures, using clearly defined measurement boundaries. Compare results with the design model across seasons, accounting for weather and occupancy. Investigate unexpected backup use, declining heat transfer or leaks. Final sizing, savings and lifecycle-cost conclusions should follow measured demand, site assessment, supplier proposals and verified energy prices."}
